educational.topic: Fan laws: speed, size and density changes
learningObjectives: Solve fan-law problems for a new speed, pressure or brake horsepower after a change in speed, impeller diameter or air density, to within 2% of the model value.

simulation.modelType: Mathematical (fan laws applied point by point to a fan curve)
assumptions: Curve A is illustrative (Chapter 10), standard air, 1,380 RPM
Geometrically similar fans; static efficiency unchanged at corresponding points
System curve P = 4.0 x (Q/10,000)^2 with no fixed pressure component, scaled by density ratio
limitations: Real product sizes are not perfectly similar; catalog or selection software governs for an order
With a diameter change the corresponding point is shown, not the intersection with the system curve

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Practice with check (commit a number before the result is revealed), then guided exploration
keyQuestions: Why does a 15% airflow increase need 52% more power?
Why does efficiency stay at 70% when only speed changes?
Why does lighter air leave CFM unchanged?
commonMisconceptions: Power rises in proportion to speed
Doubling the diameter doubles the airflow
Changing speed changes the fan's efficiency on a pure-resistance system
Hotter, lighter air changes the CFM a fan moves
assessmentOpportunities: Four challenges answered within 2% of the model value; mastery is 4 of 4
